opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about this a lot, and honestly my answer has changed over the years.

When I was starting out as a PhD student, I didn't think of it as "high-risk, high-return." I just worked on things I found genuinely interesting and that I believed would matter if they worked. Looking back, the best projects I was part of came from noticing a gap. Something was clearly going to be important, but the tools or systems to make it practical didn't exist yet. Machine learning systems was like that for a while. Lots of people cared about models, and fewer people cared about how to make them actually run well across different hardware and environments. That gap felt risky at the time, because it wasn't obviously a "research topic" in the traditional sense. But it turned out to be where a lot of leverage was.

So one heuristic I use is to ask: if this works, does it change what other people can do? I don't just mean whether it makes a paper or improves a benchmark by a few percent. I mean whether it opens a door for many other people. If the answer is yes, I'm willing to tolerate a lot of uncertainty about whether it will work.

The second thing is that "high-risk" doesn't have to mean "all-or-nothing." I try to structure a big bet so there are useful intermediate milestones along the way. You build something that's useful even if the grand vision doesn't fully pan out. Open source helps a lot here, because when you put a system out early, real users tell you very quickly whether you're solving a real problem. That feedback loop lowers the risk without lowering the ambition.

The third thing is about timing and conviction. Often a direction looks risky because it's a little too early. Hardware isn't there yet, or the models aren't there yet. I try to think about trends that are likely to hold. Compute is going to get more diverse, models are going to get bigger, and people will want to run AI everywhere, not just in a big data center. If I'm fairly confident about the trend, then working slightly ahead of it is a reasonable bet, even if it feels lonely at first.

Finally, I'd say pick problems you'd be happy to have spent years on even if the outcome is modest. Research takes a long time. If you genuinely enjoy the problem and the people you're working with, the risk feels much smaller. And you tend to do your best work when you're not constantly worrying about whether it's going to pay off.

r001.rationale: The response discusses tolerating uncertainty and structuring risky projects, but does not say that prior failures make another failure feel less daunting.

r002.rationale: It recommends choosing problems one would be happy to work on for years, but does not cite limited time as the reason.

r003.rationale: It says a personally enjoyable problem can still be worthwhile if the outcome is modest, but does not clearly state that impact is unnecessary.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about it less as "picking the riskiest thing" and more as asking what would actually matter if it worked. When I started on XGBoost, gradient boosting was not fashionable. Deep learning was taking off, and most people thought trees were a solved, boring problem. But I could see that if I built a system that was fast, scalable, and easy to use, a lot of practitioners would benefit immediately. The risk was that nobody would care. The return, if it worked, was that it would become a tool people reach for every day. So the first question is: if this succeeds, does the world look different? If the answer is no, the risk is not worth taking.

The second thing is that I try to pick directions where the risk is in execution rather than in the premise. With TVM, the premise was fairly clear to me: machine learning models were going to run on more and more kinds of hardware, and hand-writing kernels for every operator on every chip does not scale. That is a bet I was confident in. The hard part was whether we could actually build a compiler stack that generated code competitive with hand-tuned libraries. That is a risk I can reduce by working harder and iterating. I prefer that kind of risk to the kind where you only find out at the end whether the whole idea made sense.

The third thing is to build so that you learn early. A lot of so-called high-risk research is high-risk because people spend two years in isolation before anyone touches it. I like to get something end-to-end working quickly, even if it is ugly, and put it in front of real users. Open source is great for this. People show up with workloads you never imagined, and that feedback tells you whether you are on a path that matters or just one that is intellectually interesting to you.

And honestly, I also follow taste. Some of the best directions start from a feeling that the existing way of doing things is unnecessarily painful. When something annoys me enough, and I can see a cleaner abstraction underneath, that is usually a sign there is something real there. The payoff is uncertain, but the problem is real, and real problems tend to reward you eventually, even if not in the form you expected.

r001.rationale: The response discusses risk and execution, but does not say that experience with many failures makes another failure feel less daunting.

r002.rationale: The response mentions personal taste, but gives no limited-time reason for pursuing personally desired research.

r003.rationale: The response says a direction should matter if it succeeds and that real problems tend to reward effort; it does not say personally desired research is worth choosing even without impact.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to separate how important a problem is from how confident you are that your current approach will work. You can have a strong conviction that a problem matters while being quite uncertain about the solution. That uncertainty is where research comes in.

Then I would ask: what is the smallest experiment that could teach us something meaningful? A direction might have a very ambitious long-term goal, but you still want steps that let you test your assumptions. If an experiment fails, does it help you understand the problem better, or does it just leave you in the same place?

I also think it helps to have a balance. Some projects can give you steady progress and build the tools or understanding you need. Others can be more speculative. You want enough room to pursue something that might take a while, without requiring every idea to succeed immediately.

So I wouldn’t choose a direction simply because it is risky. I would choose it because the problem matters, there is a reason to believe progress is possible, and the process of trying will teach us something valuable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from failed experiments, but does not say that past failures make another failure feel less daunting.

r002.rationale: It does not cite limited time as a reason to pursue research one personally wants to do.

r003.rationale: It does not say personally desired research is worth choosing even without impact.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one useful question is: if this works, what would it enable? A direction can be very uncertain, but if success would open up something important, then it may be worth exploring. At the same time, being risky by itself doesn’t make a problem interesting. You need some reason to believe there’s an opportunity to make progress.

Then I would try to find a small experiment that tests the key assumption. You don’t have to commit several years before getting any feedback. You can keep the long-term ambition while taking concrete steps that help you learn whether the direction makes sense.

And I think personal interest matters. If you’re going to work through a lot of uncertainty, you need to care about the problem itself, not just the potential outcome.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty and testing assumptions, but does not say that prior experience with failures makes another failure less daunting.

r002.rationale: It says personal interest matters, but does not cite limited time as a reason to pursue personally desired research.

r003.rationale: It emphasizes caring about the problem, but does not state that personally desired research can be worth choosing even without impact.
